title: Wildcard Objectives — biweekly lab
content:
Purpose:
This is a two-week scratchpad for an experimental approach to personal OKRs: introduce 1–2 'wildcard' objectives that are intentionally low-probability/high-upside, alongside a stable set of committed objectives. The goal is to surface optional bets without derailing core commitments.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- Cadence: 2 weeks. Each cycle: plan (day 0), mid-check (day 7), retro (day 14).
- Structure: 3 committed objectives (C1..C3) + up to 2 wildcard objectives (W1..W2).
- Each objective gets: target metric, leading indicators, timebox, probability/confidence, and exit criteria.

This doc is intentionally messy — notes, micro-tasks, and confidence estimates.

---
Committed Objectives (C): stable, non-negotiable for the cycle
C1: Reduce mean PR review turnaround (personal)
- Target: average time from PR open to first review <= 24h for any PR I author/own.
- Leading indicators: set weekly review hours blocked on calendar (3 x 30min slots), ping two reviewers on day 1 for PRs > 6 changed files.
- Timebox: 2-week cycle.
- Confidence: 80%
- Exit criteria: maintained for 2 cycles or backlog grows >5 PRs.

C2: Ship two infra/ops improvements that lower friction for teammates
- Target: 2 merged PRs with release notes and one demo.
- Leading indicators: draft one RFC by day 4, get at least one reviewer assigned by day 8.
- Timebox: finish PRs and demos within cycle.
- Confidence: 60%

C3: Focused learning — 6 hours on kernel-level inference optimizations
- Target: 6h logged in learning notes, 1 short writeup with 3 actionable ideas for our serving runtime.
- Leading indicators: schedule 3 x 2h deep work slots; pick two papers to read.
- Timebox: 2-week cycle.
- Confidence: 70%

---
Wildcard Objectives (W): optional bets — low probability, high upside. If they start consuming stable objective time, defer or deprioritize.
W1: Prototype a tiny 'batcher-sim' microservice to explore dynamic batching heuristics
- Target: PoC that simulates duty cycles and shows at least a 10% cost win in synthetic workload within 1 day of runs.
- Leading indicators: mock traffic harness ready by day 3, 1st simulation run by day 5.
- Timebox: 7 days; if no credible delta by day 7, archive.
- Probability of success: 25%
- Upside: if it works, file a proposal for infra-owned pilot and present to serving-runtime.

W2: Cold outreach experiment — 10 targeted notes to plug into product feedback loop
- Target: 10 short convos or replies with clear new idea signals (at least 2 concrete product requests).
- Leading indicators: craft a micro template by day 2, send 5 notes by day 4.
- Timebox: 10 days; archive if <2 replies.
- Probability: 40%

---
Allocation rules (how I split time this cycle):
- Week A (days 0–6): 70% committed objectives, 30% wildcard exploration (only if indicators move).
- Week B (days 7–13): 80% committed, 20% wildcard (or zero if W hasn't shown traction).
- If W1 shows a simulation with >=5% improvement before day 6, shift an additional 10% capacity to it and notify collaborators.

Signals and metrics (personal, small and pragmatic):
- PR turnarounds (C1): track PRs opened this cycle, time-to-first-review median.
- Merge velocity (C2): PRs merged and blockers recorded.
- Learning (C3): hours tracked + number of note entries (min 3).
- Wildcard pulse: number of experiments run, credible leads produced, and whether any downstream tickets created.

Mid-cycle check (day 7) — quick checklist to run:
- PRs opened this cycle: __ (fill in)
- Median time-to-first-review: __
- Infra PRs drafted: __, reviewers assigned: __
- Learning hours logged: __
- W1 simulation status: not started / running / promising / dead
- W2 outreach replies: __ /10

Notes to self (stream-of-consciousness):
- Keep a list of tiny reminders to avoid context-switch cost: reply templates, quick triage heuristics, two-sentence summaries for each PR.
- If I feel overwhelmed, pause W2. It's reversible (no deployable code).
- Remember to batch synchronous meetings into Tue/Thu afternoons to preserve deep work mornings.
- Keep the morning 90-minute slot sacred for C3 deep work.

Mini-retro promises for next cycle (if this cycle mostly succeeds):
- Remove one wildcard and replace with a 'stretch committed' objective that is scoped smaller.
- Turn W1 into an RFC only if simulation shows >=10% improvement on median latency/cost tradeoff.

Open questions / risks:
- Risk: wildcard distraction. Mitigation: pre-committed allocation percentages and a calendar rule (no wildcard meetings unless queued on Friday).
- Risk: overstating learning time (hours don't equal focus quality). Mitigation: force 3x concise notes per 2 learning hours.
- Question: Should wildcard success create an immediate pause on C3? I think no — keep learning stable for long-term leverage.

Micro-tasks (next 48h):
- [ ] block 3 x 30m review slots on calendar (C1)
- [ ] draft infra RFC outline (C2)
- [ ] schedule 3 x 2h deep work blocks and mark them focus (C3)
- [ ] sketch W1 sim harness in notebook and list inputs (W1)
- [ ] write outreach template and list 20 contacts split into 2 cohorts (W2)

Reference bookmarks and crumbs:
- GitHub PR template: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md
- Note to self: capture simulation input distribution — seq len, arrival processes, cost model (g/gpu-min).
- Slack thread to ping for early reviewers: #infra-reviewers (ping Maya on thread)

Archive policy for this doc:
- If this cycle ends with no committed exits and no wildcard traction, keep it as 'lab' for 3 more cycles, then fold lessons into recurring one-pager and archive.

Short reflection (end-of-cycle draft placeholder):
- What surprised me? __
- Biggest friction? __
- If I could only do one thing next cycle, it would be: __

End of scratchpad. Keep minimal formatting — this is meant for quick capture, iteration, and copy/paste into Confluence when polished.
